name: Malayalam
variety: Standard Malayalam (educated speech of central Kerala), formal style
sources: Namboodiripad, Savithry and Garellek, Marc (2017). Malayalam (Namboodiri Dialect). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 47(1) (Illustrations of the IPA).
Asher, R. E. and Kumari, T. C. (1997). Malayalam. London: Routledge (Descriptive Grammars).
Mohanan, K. P. and Mohanan, Tara (1984). Lexical phonology of the consonant system in Malayalam. Linguistic Inquiry 15(4).
Mohanan, K. P. (1986). The Theory of Lexical Phonology. Dordrecht: Reidel.
Ladefoged, Peter and Maddieson, Ian (1996). The Sounds of the World's Languages. Oxford: Blackwell.
Punnoose, Reenu; Khattab, Ghada; Al-Tamimi, Jalal (2013). The contested fifth liquid in Malayalam: a window into the lateral-rhotic relationship in Dravidian languages. Phonetica 70(4).
Local, John and Simpson, Adrian P. (1999). Phonetic implementation of geminates in Malayalam nouns. Proceedings of the 14th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, San Francisco.
Jensen, Paul J. and Menon, K. M. N. (1972). Physical analysis of linguistic vowel duration. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 52.
Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju (2003). The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Féry, Caroline (2010). Indian languages as intonational 'phrase languages'. In Hasnain and Chaudhary (eds.), Problematizing Language Studies: Festschrift for Rama Kant Agnihotri. Delhi: Aakar Books.
contrasts: six places of articulation in nasals: bilabial, dental, alveolar, retroflex, palatal, velar /m n̪ n ɳ ɲ ŋ/; all six contrast as geminates between vowels (Ladefoged and Maddieson 1996 give a six-word set, with dental pʌn̪n̪i 'pig' against alveolar kʌnni 'virgin')

six places in stops and affricates: bilabial, dental, alveolar, retroflex, palato-alveolar, velar; the alveolar stop /t/ occurs only as the geminate [tː] (written റ്റ) and after /n/ (written ന്റ, pronounced [nd]); palatalised velars after front vowels are counted as a seventh place by Mohanan and Mohanan (1984)
the dental and the alveolar nasal are both written ന in the ordinary script
voiceless, voiceless aspirated, voiced and breathy voiced stops; the aspirated series belong to the Sanskrit vocabulary
five liquids: tap /ɾ/ (ര), trill /r/ (റ), alveolar lateral /l/, retroflex lateral /ɭ/, retroflex approximant /ɻ/ (ഴ)
vowel length for five vowel qualities
single versus geminate consonants, including all nasals and laterals
allophony: single voiceless stops of the native vocabulary are voiced and lax between vowels and voiced after nasals: /k/ is [ɡ] or [ɣ], /t̪/ is [d̪] or [ð], /ʈ/ is [ɖ], /p/ is [b] or [β]; after a nasal /tʃ/ is [dʒ]
the tap /ɾ/ is advanced and palatalised ('clear'), the trill /r/ is retracted and velarised ('dark'); neighbouring vowels are fronted by the first and backed and lowered by the second
/ɻ/ is a frictionless retroflex (sublaminal post-alveolar) approximant with a low third formant and clear resonance
a word-final consonant other than the sonorants /m n ɳ l ɭ ɾ/ is followed by the very short unrounded vowel [ɨ̆] or [ə̆] (samvr̥tōkāram, written with the virama and listed here as /ə/)
short /a/ is [ɐ] in the first syllable and closer to [ə] in later syllables
velar stops are palatalised after front vowels, most clearly the geminate ([kʲː])
historical nasal plus stop clusters appear as geminate nasals ([ŋŋ], [ɲɲ], [nn])
anusvara is [m] word-finally and homorganic with a following stop
breathy voiced stops are often realised as plain voiced or as voiceless aspirated stops
word-initial /e eː/ take a [j] on-glide and /o oː/ a [ʋ] on-glide
phonotactics: words end in a vowel, in the epenthetic [ɨ̆], or in one of /m n ɳ l ɭ ɾ j/

the alveolar stop occurs only geminate or after /n/; the alveolar and dental nasals contrast only as geminates between vowels, elsewhere the dental is word-initial and before dental stops and the alveolar occurs in other positions
/ɳ ɭ ɻ/ do not occur word-initially; /ɲ/ and /n̪/ do
initial clusters come from Sanskrit and English (pr-, kr-, st-, sv-)
single and geminate obstruents contrast between vowels and after sonorants; the single stop is voiced or lax there, the geminate voiceless and tense

stress.rule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable, unless that syllable has a short vowel and the second a long vowel, in which case it falls on the second; remaining long vowels take secondary stress (Mohanan 1986).
stress.cues: pitch (low on the primary stressed syllable with a rise after it) and duration; intensity differences are small

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: short /a/ is centralised toward [ə] outside the stressed syllable; other vowels keep their quality
rhythm.notes: Syllable-timed is the traditional label. Because vowel and consonant length are contrastive, syllable duration follows the number of moras. No instrumental rhythm classification or nPVI value is cited here.

length.notes: Long vowels are about twice as long as short vowels (Jensen and Menon 1972). Geminates are much longer than single consonants and also differ in voicing, tenseness and the quality of the neighbouring vowels (Local and Simpson 1999).

intonation.declarative: each non-final phrase starts low and rises to a high at its right edge; the final phrase, normally the verb, falls to low
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the clitic -ō on the verb or on the questioned word, with statement word order; pitch rises on the long clitic vowel
intonation.wh_question: question word stays in place and carries the main peak, followed by a fall to low
intonation.continuation: rise to a high boundary at the end of non-final phrases and non-finite clauses
intonation.accent_shape: LH per phrase: low on the stressed (usually first) syllable, rise to a phrase-final high
intonation.notes: Treated as a 'phrase language' by Féry (2010): tones mark phrase edges. Instrumental work on Malayalam question intonation is sparse.

phonation: breathy voiced (voiced aspirated) stops /bʱ d̪ʱ ɖʱ dʒʱ ɡʱ/ in Sanskrit vocabulary, often weakened

problems: word-medial k, t and p are silent: in ph_malayalam these phonemes import a base phoneme and then add conditions for the start and end of the word, which leaves no sound for the middle of the word; the geminates ക്ക, ത്ത, പ്പ come out as a bare silent gap with no burst or formant transitions, and the words അക്ക, അത്ത, അപ്പ give byte-identical audio
ഴ /ɻ/ is phoneme r., the base retroflex flap (r3/@tap_rfx), not an approximant; it has no IPA name, so --ipa prints 'r.'
റ്റ is rendered as retroflex [ʈʈ], which merges the alveolar geminate [tː] with ട്ട, and the rule drops the inherent vowel after it (പാറ്റ gives [paːʈʈ], മാറ്റം [maːʈʈm])
there is no dental nasal: ന is always the alveolar base n, so the dental and alveolar nasals are not distinguished and ന്ത has an alveolar nasal
word-initial /p t̪ k/ call the English base phonemes p, t, k, which are aspirated, and the /t̪/ becomes alveolar

a word-final single stop letter with virama (ക് ട് ത് പ്) gets no epenthetic vowel: monosyllables keep a voiceless stop (അത് gives [ɐt], പന്ത് [pɐnt], വീട് [viːʈ]) and longer words end in a bare voiced stop
post-nasal voicing covers ക ട ത പ but not ച (ഇഞ്ചി gives [iɲci])
anusvara is always [m], also before stops
good: the stress rule (first syllable unless it is short and the second long) follows Mohanan's description, with equal stress amplitudes
tap ര and trill റ are distinct, and ന്റ is alveolar [nd]
single stops are voiced between vowels and after nasals; vowel length is kept and geminates get a long closure
the final epenthetic vowel [ɨ] is produced after a sonorant or geminate with virama; unstressed short a is reduced to [ə]

notes: The ordinary script does not separate the dental from the alveolar nasal, so a text-to-speech system needs a lexicon or positional rules (dental word-initially and before dental stops) to place them.
